mals being hardly distinguished in the
common usage of the Hebrew. Gen. 49,
21. Plur. אַיָּלוֹת constr. אַיְלוֹת 2 Sam. 22,
34. Cant. 2, 7. See in masc. אַיָּל.
אַיָּלוֹן (from אַיָּל, q. d. Deerfield, from
the number of deer,) Ajalon, pr. n. a)
A Levitical city in the tribe of Dan,
See Bibl. Res. in Palest. III. p. 63. b)
A city in Zebulun, Judg. 12, 12.
אֵילוֹן (an oak, see אַלּוֹן) Elon, pr. n.
1. A city in Dan, Josh. 19, 43. 1 K.
2. Of several men: a) Gen. 26, 34.
אֵילוֹת (trees, a grove, perh. palm-
grove, see under אֵלָה) 1 K. 9, 26. 2 K.
16, 6, also אֵילַת (for אֵילָה Lehrg. p. 467,
and that collect. for אֵילוֹת) Deut. 2, 8.
2 K. 14, 22. 16, 6 bis, Eloth, Elath, pr. n.
of a city of Idumea on the eastern gulf
of the Red Sea, which is called from it
Sinus Ælanites, or Elanitic Gulf. The
Edomites being subdued, 2 Sam. 8, 14,
David took possession of it, and after
him Solomon, whose fleet sailed hence
to Ophir, 1 K. 9, 26. It was again recov-
ered by the Idumeans; and once more
subdued by Uzziah king of Judah, 2 K.
14, 22; but Rezin king of Syria took it
at length from the Jews, who seem never
again to have recovered it, 2 K. 16, 6.
Josephus calls it Εἰλάνη, Ptolemy Ἔλανα,
Pliny Ælana H. N. 6. 32 or 38. See
Relandi Palæst. p. 217, 554 sq. Le
Quien Oriens Christ. T. III. p. 758. By
Arabian writers it is called أَيْلَةُ Aileh,
Ailat. The ruins of the former city are
still visible near to the fortress of ’Aka-
bah, on the N. W. Rüppell’s Reisen,
p. 248 seq. Frankf. 1829. Bibl. Res. in
Palest. I. p. 241 sq.
אֱיָלוּת f. i. q. אֱיָל pr. strength, might,
then help, Ps. 22, 20. R. אוּל no. 2.
אֵילָם plur. אֵילַמִּים and אֵלַמּוֹת, an ar-
chitectural term, which the Sept. Vulg.
and Targums make i. q. אוּלָם porch;
from which however it is manifestly
distinguished, Ez. 40, 7 sq. The אֵילַמִּים
were carried round an edifice, and are
usually mentioned along with the אֱלִילִים;
see Ez. 40, 16. 22. 26. 29. Comp. Boett-
cher Proben, p. 319.
אֵילִם (trees, perh. palm-trees) Elim,
pr. n. of a station of the Israelites in the
desert, the second after leaving Egypt,
with twelve fountains and seventy palm-
trees, Ex. 15, 27. 16, 1. Num. 33, 9. With
He loc. אֵילִמָה Ex. 15, 27.—Geographers
rightly assume the place of Elim in the
Wady Ghŭrŭndel, a valley of that re-
gion; see Bibl. Res. in Palest. I. p. 100,
אִילָן Chald. m. a tree, Dan. 4, 7. 8 sq.
Syr. ܐܺܝܠܳܢܳܐ id. It corresponds to Heb.
אַלּוֹן; but the Chaldee word is used in a
wider sense.
אֵילַת see in אֵילוֹת.
אַיֶּלֶת f. i. q. אַיָּלָה (to which it is also
st. constr.) a hind, as a term of endear-
ment towards a female, Prov. 5, 19.—
More difficult of explanation is it in the
inscription of Ps. 22 עַל־אַיֶּלֶת הַשַּׁחַר upon
(according to) the hind of the dawn.
These words seem to be the name of
some other poem or song, to the measure
of which this Psalm was to be sung or
chanted; comp. קֶשֶׁת 2 Sam. 1, 18. The
phrase hind of the dawn prob. stands for
the morning sun scattering his first rays
upon the earth; just as the Arabian po-
ets call the rising sun the gazelle, com-
paring his rays with the horns of that
animal; comp. קֶרֶן lett. e. See Schultens
ad Job. p. 1193; ad Har. Cons. V. p. 163.
* אָיַם obsol. root, Chald. and Tal-
mud. אֲיֵם, to terrify. The primary idea
seems to be to strike dumb; comp. r.
הָמַם, דָּהַם; perh. also צָרַם q. v.—Hence
the two following:
אָיֹם adj. f. אֲיֻמָּה, terrible, formidable,
אֵימָה and אֵמָה f. (for אֲיֻמָּה) terror,
dread, Deut. 32, 25. With genit. of that
which inspires terror; Prov. 20, 2 אֵימַת
מֶלֶךְ the dread of a king, which one feels
before him. Job 33, 7 אֵימָתִי the terror of
me, i. e. which I inspire. With He parag.
אֵימָתָה Ex. 15, 16. Plur. אֵימוֹת Ps. 55, 5.
Plur. אֵימִים 1. terrors, Ps. 88, 16.
2. idols Jer. 50, 38, so called from the
terror with which they inspire their
worshippers. Comp. מִפְּלֶצֶת.

line_status.note: The printed word has two lameds (א‑ל‑י‑ל‑י‑ם, "idols") with a ḥateph segol under the aleph, not אֵילִים with tsere; a thin space is printed before the semicolon.

The third Hebrew word begins with a tsade (צ, with its characteristic diagonal arm), not ayin, and its middle letter is full-height with a flat top bar — a resh (ר), not a short yod. Points under it are qamets, patach; הָמַם and דָּהַם with dagesh in daleth agree in both readings and match the print.

Under the yod of the parenthetical form the print shows a diagonal row of three dots (qibbuts), matching the adjective אֲיֻמָּה in line 1, not a single qamets; dagesh is visible in the mem. Reading B is correct.
The Hebrew is printed plene: a yod is clearly visible between the aleph (with tsere) and the mem (with qamets), matching the plene אֵימַת in line 1 above; Reading A drops it.

The pe clearly carries a dagesh (dot inside the letter) in the print, so Reading B's מִפְּלֶצֶת is correct; A omits it. Vowels otherwise agree: hireq under mem, sheva under pe, segol under lamed and tsade, no plene vav/yod.
